table.text: Participants were asked whether they had ever experienced: (a) physical abuse by an intimate partner, such as slapping, punching, kicking, pushing, biting, hair pulling, assault with objects or weapons, confinement, physical restraint, strangulation, or suffocation; (b) psychological/emotional abuse, including ridicule, persistent criticism, humiliation, threats, blackmail, bullying, gaslighting, or excessive control over personal activities, financial resources, social interactions, or physical appearance; and (c) sexual abuse, encompassing any form of non-consensual sexual contact, rape, sexual harassment, or coercive sexting.
Participants are instructed to consider various dimensions of their sleep experience, including sleep duration, ease of sleep initiation, frequency of awakenings, and the restorative nature of sleep.
Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants before accessing the questionnaire through the selection of an "I agree to participate" option.
More than half of the participants were either married or cohabiting with a partner (55.3%), while 42.1% were singles, 1.8% were divorced, and 0.9% were widowed.
The vast majority of participants were employed (92.9%).
Second, males were recruited through a non-probability convenience sampling strategy using social media platforms.

METHODS A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in Greece in July 2026.

IPV among males was assessed using the Woman Abuse Screening Tool (WAST), while the lifetime prevalence of physical, psychological/emotional, and sexual abuse was evaluated through three dichotomous self-report items (yes/no).
Anxiety-like and depressive-like symptoms were measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4).

Sleep quality was assessed with the Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale (SQS), self-esteem with the Single-Item Self-Esteem Scale (SISE), loneliness with the UCLA 3-Item Loneliness Scale (UCLA-LS-3), and life satisfaction with the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS).
To account for the potential influence of demographic characteristics, multivariable linear regression analyses were performed with adjustment for relevant demographic confounding variables.
RESULTS In the adjusted model, higher levels of males' abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of anxiety-like symptoms.
Additionally, levels of anxiety-like symptoms were higher among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives.
Multivariable model found that higher levels of males' abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of depressive-like symptoms.
Additionally, levels of depressive-like symptoms were higher among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives.
Sleep quality was worse among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives.
Higher levels of males' abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with lower levels of self-esteem.
Additionally, levels of self-esteem were lower among males that have experienced physical abuse through their lives.
Higher levels of males' abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of loneliness.
Higher levels of males' abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with lower levels of life satisfaction.
Additionally, levels of life satisfaction were lower among males that have experienced psychological/emotional abuse through their lives.
CONCLUSIONS IPV was significantly associated with poorer mental health and psychosocial well-being among males in Greece.

Greater exposure to abusive behaviors was associated with higher levels of anxiety-like symptoms, depressive-like symptoms, and loneliness, as well as poorer sleep quality, lower self-esteem, and reduced life satisfaction.
These findings highlight the substantial psychological burden associated with IPV and underscore its detrimental impact on multiple dimensions of mental health and well-being among male victims.

Intimate partner violence (IPV) is recognized globally as a significant public health issue and encompasses any behavior occurring within intimate relationships that causes physical, sexual or psychological harm to the victims. 1, 2 Over the past few decades, scientific literature has predominantly focused on females as victims and males as perpetrators, [3] [4] [5] [6] leaving male victimization noticeably understudied. [7] [8] [9] Consequently, public health initiatives, legal frameworks, and support services have primarily centered around violence against women. 1, 10, 11 However, emerging evidence is revealing that men also experience substantial rates of IPV. [7] [8] [9] [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] Despite this growing recognition, determining the exact prevalence of male victimization remains challenging, as rates vary widely depending on study methodology, geographical context, and how IPV is defined. 20 Globally, general estimates suggest that between 17% and 20% of men experience IPV during their lifetime. 7 Providing a closer examination of these figures, a review of 34 studies on male IPV victimization, by Nowinski and Bowen (2012) found that lifetime prevalence rates for heterosexual men ranged from 7.3% to 32.4%, while 12-month prevalence spanned between 0.6% and 29.3% across all forms of violence. 21 Importantly, these global estimates mask significant regional and cultural variations.

text.text: Evidence indicates that men most frequently experience psychological violence, followed by physical, and, to a lesser extent, sexual violence. 7, 13, 15 To provide empirical context to these figures, recent analyses of the World Health Organization (WHO) global dataset, comprising over 600 data points, indicate that approximately 9% of IPV studies focus on male victims. 13 Within this subset, the median lifetime prevalences reported for men reach 24.4% for psychological abuse, 17.1% for physical abuse, and 13.0% for sexual abuse. 13 Furthermore, help-seeking behavior differs markedly by gender, with men being substantially less likely to report their abuse or access support services than women. 13, 18 This lack of disclosure masks the actual scope of male victimization, often leading institutional stakeholders to dismiss the issue as a minor problem. 7, 22 A primary internal barrier driving this silence is men's failure to self-identify as victims or recognize their experiences as IPV. 7, 15, 17, 18 This reluctance to identify as a victim is deeply rooted in traditional masculine norms, which dictate that men must remain strong, stoic, emotionally controlled, and self-reliant. 7, 8, 15, 18 Consequently, acknowledging victimization is often perceived as weak or "unmanly", leading male victims to internalize their trauma through profound feelings of shame, embarrassment, guilt, and denial. 13, 15, 18, 22 Beyond these internal struggles, male victims face severe external and institutional barriers, most notably societal stigma and a pervasive fear of not being believed. 8, 13, 22 Because society and institutional networks are often predisposed to stereotype men as aggressive perpetrators and women as fragile victims, men fear that disclosing their abuse will result in their experiences being minimized, ignored, or resulting in false accusations that they are the actual abusers. 7, 13, 15, 17 Unfortunately, these fears are frequently validated by negative institutional responses, as men who report their abuse to police or support services are often mocked, told to "man up", ridiculed, or even arrested. 7, 13, 22 In addition, many men remain in abusive relationships or tolerate the violence to protect their partner, maintain family relationships, or out of fear of retaliation and losing custody of their children. 7, 13, 18 Because of this complex set of barriers, when men do decide to seek help, they rely predominantly on informal networks, such as friends and family, rather than formal public resources, which they frequently evaluate as unhelpful. 15, 18 Finally, evidence suggests that men rarely seek help unless physical violence is involved, underscoring the need to support victims of nonphysical forms of IPV, such as psychological or emotional abuse. 18 International research reveals severe, multi-dimensional consequences of IPV on male victims.

text.text: The absence of culturally and geographically relevant data hinders the development of inclusive social policies, specialized clinical guidelines, and targeted support services for men experiencing IPV in the country.
In this context, we conducted a cross-sectional study to examine the association between IPV and multiple dimensions of mental health in a sample of males in Greece.
To the best of our knowledge, the present study is the first to address this important research gap in the Greek population.
A cross-sectional survey was conducted in Greece in July 2026 using an online data collection approach.
Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire created with Google Forms and disseminated via multiple social media platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and LinkedIn.
The study population consisted of males with internet access who actively engaged with social media.
Participation was voluntary, and no financial or material incentives were offered.
Participants selfenrolled by accessing the survey link and completing the questionnaire.
Eligibility criteria required participants to be males, to have been in an intimate relationship for at least the preceding 12 months, and to provide informed consent before participation.
Recruitment was based on a non-probability convenience sampling approach, resulting in the acquisition of a convenience sample.

The study was conducted and reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. 24 To reduce selection bias, the participant information sheet described the study as an examination of intimate partner relationships without explicitly referring to abusive behaviors toward males.

text.text: This approach was intended to promote participation among males regardless of their exposure to IPV, thereby minimizing the likelihood of disproportionate recruitment of individuals with victimization experiences.
Consequently, the risk of overestimating the prevalence of abusive behaviors within the sample was reduced.
Sample size estimation was performed using G*Power software (version 3.1.9.2).
The calculation was based on a multivariable analytical model incorporating 10 variables, including four independent predictors and six potential confounding factors.
Assuming a conservative small effect size (f² = 0.05), a significance level of 0.05, and a statistical power of 95%, the minimum required sample size was estimated at 262 males.

The adoption of a conservative effect size was intended to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting small, yet potentially meaningful, associations between the predictor variables and the study outcomes.

Demographic information was collected from participants, including age (continuous variable), marital status (single, married, cohabiting with a partner, divorced, or widowed), number of children (continuous variable), educational attainment (elementary school, high school, or college degree), and employment status (employed vs. unemployed).

In addition, perceived economic status was assessed using a self-reported rating scale ranging from 0 (very poor) to 10 (excellent), with higher scores indicating more favorable perceptions of economic well-being.

IPV was assessed using the Woman Abuse Screening Tool (WAST). 25, 26 The WAST is a validated instrument designed to identify emotional, physical, and sexual abuse among males in intimate relationships, facilitating the early detection of abuse and appropriate referral to specialized support services.

text.text: The instrument consists of eight items rated on a three-point Likert scale, with response options ranging from never (0) to often (2).
Total scores range from 0 to 16, with higher scores indicating greater exposure to abusive behaviors.

Consistent with the cut-off score recommended by the instrument's developers, participants with a total WAST score of ≥5 were classified as likely to be experiencing IPV, whereas those scoring <5 were considered unlikely to be victims of abuse.

text.text: The lifetime prevalence of IPV was evaluated using three self-reported dichotomous items (yes/no) assessing experiences of physical, psychological/emotional, and sexual abuse.

Participants were asked whether they had ever experienced: (a) physical abuse by an intimate partner, such as slapping, punching, kicking, pushing, biting, hair pulling, assault with objects or weapons, confinement, physical restraint, strangulation, or suffocation; (b) psychological/emotional abuse, including ridicule, persistent criticism, humiliation, threats, blackmail, bullying, gaslighting, or excessive control over personal activities, financial resources, social interactions, or physical appearance; and (c) sexual abuse, encompassing any form of non-consensual sexual contact, rape, sexual harassment, or coercive sexting.
Responses were recorded as either yes or no for each category of abuse.

The lifetime prevalence of physical, psychological/emotional, and sexual IPV was calculated as the proportion of males reporting a positive response for each respective type of abuse within the study sample.

Anxiety-like and depressive-like symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4), a brief self-report screening tool comprising four items, including two items evaluating anxiety-like symptoms and two items assessing depressive-like symptoms. 28 It should be noted that the PHQ-4 measures symptoms suggestive of anxiety and depression rather than providing clinical diagnoses or directly assessing anxiety and depressive disorders.

text.text: Responses are rated on a fourpoint Likert scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day).
Subscale scores for anxiety-like and depressive-like symptoms range from 0 to 6, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.

The validated Greek version of the PHQ-4 was used in the present study. 29 Internal consistency was good, with Cronbach's alpha coefficients of 0.802 for the anxiety-like symptoms subscale and 0.724 for the depressive-like symptoms subscale.

text.text: Participation was voluntary and anonymous.

Prior to participation, prospective participants received comprehensive information regarding the study aims, procedures, voluntary nature of involvement, and their right to withdraw at any stage without consequence.
Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants before accessing the questionnaire through the selection of an "I agree to participate" option.
Data collection was conducted via an anonymous online survey, and no personally identifiable information was collected.
To ensure participant privacy and confidentiality, the questionnaire was administered using a secure online platform with access restricted to authorized members of the research team.
All data were stored in password-protected files, while IP addresses and other potential indirect identifiers were not recorded.

In addition, all responses were analyzed and presented exclusively in aggregated form to minimize the risk of participant identification and to ensure adherence to applicable ethical and data protection requirements.
Categorical variables are summarized using absolute (n) and relative (%) frequencies, whereas continuous variables were described using means, standard deviations (SD),

text.text: The mean age of participants was 36.8 years (SD = 10.3), with a median age of 37 years (interquartile range = 16), ranging from 18 to 65 years.
More than half of the participants were either married or cohabiting with a partner (55.3%), while 42.1% were singles, 1.8% were divorced, and 0.9% were widowed.
Regarding family status, 35.3% of participants reported having children.
In terms of educational attainment, 92.6% of the sample held a college degree, whereas 7.4% had completed secondary (high school) education.
The vast majority of participants were employed (92.9%).
Perceived financial status, assessed on a scale ranging from 0 to 10, had a mean score of 6.5 (SD = 1.4) and a median score of 7 (IQR = 2), with observed values ranging from 0 to 9.
Psychological/emotional abuse was the most commonly reported form of IPV, followed by physical and sexual abuse.
In particular, the lifetime prevalence of physical IPV was 15.6% (n = 53), while the prevalence of psychological/emotional abuse was 50.0% (n = 170).
Sexual abuse was reported by 1.2% of males (n = 4).

text.text: Addressing a critical gap in the existing literature, the present study investigates the link between IPV and mental health outcomes among male victims in Greece.
By examining how men's exposure to IPV correlates with different aspects of their mental health and general well-being, our research aims to directly inform public health policy.
Consistent with prior research, 7, 13, 15 this study found that psychological/emotional abuse was the most commonly reported form of IPV, followed by physical and sexual abuse.

text.text: This pattern mirrors our previous findings in a female sample, where psychological violence was similarly the most frequent form of IPV. 38 Specifically, the lifetime prevalence of psychological/emotional abuse among males was 50.0%, while physical IPV was reported by 15.6% of the participants.

text.text: Sexual abuse was the least common form, reported by 1.2% of the study sample.
Furthermore, our findings reveal a robust association between male victimization and both depression-and anxiety-like symptoms.
Higher levels of recent abuse, as indicated by elevated WAST scores, correlated strongly with higher levels of these symptoms.
Notably, this effect was not limited to recent abuse.
Males who reported a lifetime history of physical and psychological/emotional abuse also exhibited significantly higher baseline levels of symptoms indicative of both anxiety and depression.
These results align with previous studies linking IPV to the development of anxiety and depression. 23, [39] [40] [41] This dual impact highlights the cumulative and enduring nature of trauma.

text.text: While recent abuse likely acts as an acute stressor that triggers immediate anxiety-and depressive-like symptomatology, lifetime exposure to physical and emotional violence appears to have a deeper impact on males' mental health by fundamentally altering the stress response system. 42 As a result, chronic trauma leads to severe psychological stress alongside endocrine and immuneinflammatory dysregulation, both of which are key drivers of depression. 42 This persistent physiological dysregulation was further reflected in reduced sleep quality.

text.text: Our analysis showed that men with a lifetime history of physical and psychological/emotional abuse reported significantly poorer sleep quality than those without such experiences.

This finding may be partly explained by the effects of chronic traumatic stress on the body's stress-response system, which sustains hyperarousal and hypervigilance, thereby interfering with normal sleep patterns. 43 Poor sleep may, in turn, further exacerbate emotional distress, creating a vicious cycle in which trauma exposure, psychological symptoms, and sleep disruption reinforce one another.

text.text: Participants who reported elevated WAST scores (recent abuse) and those who had experienced physical abuse at any point in their lives had significantly lower levels of self-esteem.
This finding requires critical interpretation within the context of traditional gender norms.

Societal expectations often dictate that men should be strong, capable of defending themselves, emotionally controlled and self-reliant. 7, 13, 15, 18 Experiencing IPV directly contradicts these internalized masculine ideals, inducing profound feelings of shame and guilt that ultimately lead to diminished confidence and reduced self-worth. 7, 13, 15, 18 Our multivariable models also showed that higher levels of recent abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with increased feelings of loneliness.

text.text: Τhis finding aligns with previous literature showing that male IPV victims frequently experience severe social isolation and heightened loneliness. 45 Specifically, recent research from Wales highlights that this loneliness and reduced psychological well-being are significantly exacerbated if fathers are separated from their children. 45 Driven by societal stigma and a pervasive fear of disbelief, male victims often suffer in silence and remain hesitant to seek help.

text.text: Consequently, this compounding burden of psychosocial and mental health consequences may considerably reduce victims' life satisfaction.
In our study, recent abuse, as assessed by the WAST score, was a predictor of lower overall life satisfaction.
Furthermore, we found a similarly detrimental effect among males who had experienced lifetime psychological/emotional abuse.

Building upon our earlier results, it is highly probable that the cumulative effects of anxiety-and depressivelike symptoms, as well as feelings of loneliness, fundamentally undermine overall well-being, ultimately driving the observed decline in life satisfaction.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study.
First, the cross-sectional design does not permit conclusions regarding the temporal sequence or causality of the observed associations between IPV and mental health outcomes.
Second, males were recruited through a non-probability convenience sampling strategy using social media platforms.
As participation was voluntary and based on self-selection, the sample may not be representative of the broader male population in Greece.
Third, because recruitment was conducted through publicly accessible online posts, the number of individuals who viewed the study invitation could not be determined.
Consequently, an accurate response rate could not be calculated, making it difficult to evaluate the potential impact of non-response bias.
Fourth, all study variables were assessed using self-report measures, which are inherently vulnerable to information bias, including recall bias and social desirability bias.

Fifth, the online methodology may have excluded certain population groups, including males with limited digital literacy, restricted internet access, older age, lower socioeconomic status, or residence in geographically remote areas.
Consequently, selection bias may have been introduced, further affecting the representativeness of the sample.
Finally, although several demographic variables were measured and considered in the analyses, residual confounding due to unmeasured factors remains possible.
Despite these limitations, the study possesses several notable strengths.

These include the use of validated instruments to assess multiple dimensions of IPV and psychological well-being, the inclusion of a relatively heterogeneous sample of males from different regions of Greece, and the examination of a topic that has received limited empirical attention in the Greek context.
To our knowledge, this study provides some of the first evidence regarding the association between IPV and mental health outcomes among males worldwide.
As such, the findings offer an important basis for future research, particularly longitudinal investigations and nationally representative studies aimed at further elucidating these associations.
In conclusion, this cross-sectional study provides evidence of significant associations between IPV and multiple dimensions of mental health and psychosocial well-being among males in Greece.

Greater exposure to abusive behaviors was associated with elevated symptoms indicative of anxiety and depression, increased loneliness, lower self-esteem, poorer sleep quality and reduced life satisfaction.

These findings highlight the psychological and psychosocial burden associated with IPV victimization among men and underscore the importance of recognizing both recent and lifetime experiences of abuse when assessing male victims' well-being.
Despite growing recognition of male IPV victimization, the experiences and support needs of male victims remain insufficiently addressed.

The findings emphasize the importance of developing inclusive, evidence-based screening and support approaches within healthcare and social care settings that acknowledge gender-related stigma and barriers to disclosure and help-seeking.

Further research, particularly using longitudinal designs, is needed to clarify the relationships between IPV exposure and psychological and psychosocial outcomes, as well as to examine the distinct effects of different forms of IPV.

By contributing to the limited evidence on IPV and mental health among males in Greece, this study highlights the need for targeted prevention strategies, appropriate clinical guidance, and accessible support services that address the complex and diverse needs of men experiencing IPV.
